Chapter 0

How to use this guide

What this volume is. This volume is a guided reading path through two books you already own. The RRK Agentic AI Textbook v2 covers 16 chapters and whiteboard method, system design, agentic design, FDE playbook, GCP stack, agents. RAG, chunking, embeddings, eval, guardrails, GPUs/serving/cost, board sessions, appendix. The RRK Interview Q&A Bank v2 holds hundreds of questions across discovery, coding, system design, agentic design, RAG, guardrails, production/cost, and behavioral. Part 1 (Chapters 1-6) teaches the foundations from zero on this page. Part 2 (Paths A-F) maps the RRK books: reading order, master/skim marks, connections to Volumes 1-8, and gaps with forward pointers.

Why it exists and The RRK books are deep and GCP-flavored. This spine is first-principles and lab-built. Read naively, you would re-learn serving math twice. You would also miss that the spine already taught the expensive parts. The six paths map RRK chapters to review topics. They pin every bridge note: the exact place where a spine volume deepens an RRK chapter, or vice versa.

How to use it. Each path has the reading order with master/skim marks. Each path has bridge notes to the spine. Each path has one worked example and the trap to avoid. Each path has a design-prompt question set with real QA Bank codes, and crisp sentences. Budget about two weeks alongside the spine.

The curriculum map suggests Volumes 9-10 take one week. Give this guide the larger share.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Top to bottom, the six paths: agents, RAG, evals, guardrails, FDE playbook, GPU and GCP stack.
  2. 2. Each box carries a side tag. Master means field-critical. Skim means learn the ideas, not the product names.
  3. 3. Arrows show the reading order. Paths A through C are the technical core. Paths D through F are the production shell.
  4. 4. Teaching point: the order is deliberate. Agents come before RAG because agentic RAG assumes the loop. Evals come before guardrails because you cannot guard what you cannot measure.
Master tags
What it is: Paths A, B, C: the field core. What breaks if it fails: Skimming these leaves you unable to answer G1-G15 or S9/S37.
Skim tags
What it is: Product-specific mappings (ADK names, GCP SKUs). What breaks if it fails: You memorize volatile product names instead of the portable pattern underneath.
Path order
What it is: The dependency chain of the guide. What breaks if it fails: Reading guardrails before evals teaches defenses for unmeasured behavior.

Key takeaways

  • Two parts: Chapters 1-6 teach the foundations from zero on this page. Paths A-F map the RRK v2 books onto them.
  • Six paths in order: agents, RAG, evals, guardrails, FDE playbook, GPU/GCP stack.
  • Bridge notes are the point. They connect RRK chapters to Volumes 2, 4, 7, 8, and forward to Volume 10.

Next: Chapter 1: what a bare LLM cannot do, and why everything in this volume fixes one of three limits.

Chapter 1

What an LLM cannot do alone

The starting point and A language model is a next-token predictor. People trained it on a pile of text. Its knowledge lives in its weights: the numbers learned during training, frozen the day training finished. Everything in this chapter follows from that one fact. Ask a bare model three kinds of questions. Watch it fail in three different ways.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Stale knowledge. A knowledge cutoff is the date the training data ends. The model knows nothing after it, by construction. Ask about anything newer. It either says it does not know or, worse, invents an answer.
  2. No actions. The model can only write text. It cannot query your database, click a link, or run code. A question like "what is the status of order 4821" is unanswerable. The answer lives in a system the model cannot touch.
  3. No private data. The model never saw your team documents, your wiki, or your files. "What did we decide in yesterday's meeting" has no answer in its weights.

Hallucination, defined. A hallucination is the model generating a confident, fluent answer that is false. It happens because people trained the model to produce plausible text, not to check facts. Stale knowledge makes hallucinations worse. When the model has no real answer, plausibility is all it has.

The context window, briefly. The context window is how much text the model can consider at once. Your question must fit inside it. Anything you want it to use must fit inside it. Its answer must fit inside it. This limit is why the fixes below cannot just "paste the whole internet in."

Key takeaways

  • A bare LLM has three hard limits: knowledge frozen at the cutoff date, no ability to act, no access to your private data.
  • Hallucination is confident falsehood. It is the default failure when the model lacks the facts.
  • The rest of this volume is the fix list. Retrieval answers stale knowledge and private data. Tools answer no-actions. Agents combine all three.

Design prompt

  1. "A user asks your assistant about an event from last week. What are the three ways a bare LLM fails, and which fix addresses each?"
  2. "Why can a model be confidently wrong about something it was never trained on? What is that failure called?"

Next: Chapter 2 answers the first limit. Keep knowledge outside the model and retrieve it when needed. The simplest fix.

Chapter 2

Retrieval: the simplest answer to stale knowledge

The simplest fix. Do not retrain the model. Keep the knowledge outside the model, in documents you control. When a question arrives, find the relevant pieces and paste them into the prompt. The model then answers from fresh text instead of frozen weights. This is the whole idea of retrieval: finding the pieces of a collection that are relevant to a question.

Terms, once and A corpus is the collection of documents you search. A document is one item in it: a page, a ticket, a wiki article. A query is the question, as text. Relevance is how well a piece answers the question. An index is the data structure that makes finding fast. It saves you from reading every document per question.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Question. The user asks in plain language. Nothing about the corpus is in the model's weights.
  2. Find relevant pages. A retriever searches the corpus. It returns the few pages most likely to answer. This is the step the rest of the chapter is about.
  3. Paste into the prompt. The prompt becomes: "Using these pages, answer this question." The pages are fresh. They can be private. They were written yesterday.
  4. Grounded answer. The answer quotes or cites the pages, so a human can check it. Stale knowledge and private data: fixed.

What this does not solve. Step 2 hides all the hard parts. How do you cut documents into findable pieces? How do you measure "relevant" without reading everything? How do you search a million pieces in milliseconds? Those are the next chapter.

Retrieval only answers questions. It does not act. Acting is Chapter 6.

Key takeaways

  • Retrieval keeps knowledge outside the model. It fetches knowledge per question. Fresh, private, checkable.
  • Corpus, document, query, relevance, index: the five words the whole field is built on.
  • The open problems all live inside step 2: cutting, measuring, and searching at scale.

Design prompt

  1. "Why is retrieval cheaper than retraining when the documents change daily? What breaks if the corpus has ten million documents?"
  2. "Your retriever returns pages but the answers are still wrong. Is the failure in step 2 or step 4? How would you tell?"

Next: Chapter 3 builds the machinery retrieval needs: chunks, embeddings, and fast search.

Chapter 3

Chunks, embeddings, and vector search

Three ideas, simplest first. Step 2 of retrieval needs machinery. It needs a way to cut documents. It needs a way to measure relevance. It needs a way to search fast. Each idea below answers one of those.

Idea 1: chunks. Documents are long and the context window is finite. You cannot paste a whole manual per question. You would not want to: the one relevant paragraph would drown. Cut each document into chunks: short passages, each about one idea. A token is the model's unit of text, roughly three quarters of a word in English.

You measure chunk sizes in tokens: a few hundred is typical. Chunks overlap: each chunk repeats a little of the previous one, so a fact sitting on a boundary survives. Every chunk keeps its source page, so answers can cite it.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Left: a document is cut into four chunks with overlap. The overlap means "within 30 days" appears in two chunks. No boundary can destroy it.
  2. Bad split (red): the fact "within 30 days of purchase" is cut in half. Neither half answers the question on its own. This chunking destroyed information. No later stage can recover it.
  3. Good split (teal): one complete idea per chunk. Retrieval can find it. The model can quote it.
  4. The trade-off: small chunks are precise but lose context. Large chunks keep context but dilute the match. Tune it with evals, not taste.
How to read this diagram.
  1. Small chunks. Precise matches. But ideas that span boundaries are lost.
  2. Large chunks. Keep context. But the match dilutes across more text.
  3. The fix. Overlap protects facts at boundaries. One idea per chunk keeps retrieval precise. Tune with evals, not taste.

Idea 2: embeddings. How do you find the chunk that answers the question without reading all of them? Turn meaning into numbers. An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. An embedding model is the small model that computes these lists and similar meanings produce similar lists. The vectors point in similar directions.

cos(θ) = (A · B) / (‖A‖ ‖B‖)

Where: A, B = the two embedding vectors; A · B = dot product (sum of pairwise products); ‖A‖ = length of A; θ = angle between them. A small angle means cos(θ) near 1: similar meaning.

Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors. A small angle means similar meaning. Real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of numbers (dimensions). The figure shows two so you can see it.

Worked example (2D, like the figure). A = (1, 0), B = (0.8, 0.6).

  1. Dot product: A · B = 1·0.8 + 0·0.6 = 0.8.
  2. Lengths: ‖A‖ = 1, ‖B‖ = √(0.64 + 0.36) = 1.
  3. cos(θ) = 0.8 / (1 · 1) = 0.8. Near 1: small angle, similar meaning. An unrelated vector like (0, 1) would score 0.
How to read this diagram.
  1. Clusters: "cat", "dog", "puppy", "kitten" land together. "car", "engine", "tire" land far away. The embedding model learned this geometry from text alone.
  2. The query "puppy" lands inside the animal cluster. Its nearest neighbors are the answer. Relevance becomes distance.
  3. Cosine similarity (inset): two arrows with a small angle between them are similar. A wide angle means unrelated. Retrieval ranks chunks by this angle.

Idea 3: vector search. Embed every chunk once and store the vectors. At query time, embed the question and find the nearest chunk vectors. Checking every vector exactly is too slow at a million chunks. Production systems use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search: an index that finds almost-the-nearest vectors far faster than checking all of them. HNSW and IVF are two popular ANN index shapes. ScaNN is Google's (trees plus quantization). A vector database stores vectors and runs ANN search, alongside the original text and metadata. Top-k means the k highest-scoring chunks: the ones you paste into the prompt.

The keyword side. Embeddings miss exact terms: product codes, names, error strings. Keyword search matches words directly. BM25 is the classic formula. It scores documents by matching words and rewarding rare ones. Hybrid search runs both vector and keyword search and merges the lists. RRF (reciprocal rank fusion) is a simple merge formula. A reranker, often a cross-encoder (a model that reads the query and one chunk together and scores the match), re-scores the top candidates precisely. It is slow, so it only ever sees the top 50, never the million.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Two searches. Vector search finds meaning. Keyword search (BM25) finds exact terms. Run both.
  2. RRF merge. Reciprocal rank fusion merges the two lists into one ranking.
  3. Reranker. A cross-encoder reads query and chunk together. Slow but accurate. Only sees top 50.

Common misunderstanding.

"Better embeddings fix bad retrieval." No. Retrieval can only find what chunking preserved. A fact cut in half at chunk time is gone. No vector quality brings it back. Fix chunking first, then the index, then the reranker.

Key takeaways

  • Chunks make documents findable. Overlap protects facts at boundaries. One idea per chunk.
  • Embeddings turn meaning into vectors. Cosine similarity turns relevance into an angle.
  • ANN search makes nearest-neighbor fast at scale. Hybrid search plus a reranker covers what vectors miss.

Design prompt

  1. "Your corpus is a million chunks. Why can you not score every chunk per query, and what does ANN give up to be fast?"
  2. "A user searches for an exact error code and vector search misses it. What do you add, and where in the pipeline?"

Next: Chapter 4 wires the retriever and the machinery into the full RAG pipeline, end to end.

Chapter 4

The RAG pipeline, end to end

RAG, defined. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) is the full pipeline: the retriever from Chapter 2 plus the machinery from Chapter 3, wired to a generator. It has two paths.

The index path runs offline, once. Documents become chunks. Chunks become embeddings. Embeddings go into the index.

The query path runs online, per question. Embed the question. Search the index. Build the prompt from the question plus the top-k chunks. Generate the answer.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Index path (offline). Documents become chunks. Chunks become embeddings. Embeddings go into the ANN index. This runs once.
  2. Query path (online). Embed the question with the same model. Search the index for top-k chunks. Build the prompt. Generate the answer.
  3. Why two paths. Indexing is expensive. You do it once. Querying is cheap. You do it per question.
How to read this diagram.
  1. Index path (teal): your corpus is cut into chunks. Each chunk is embedded. The vectors go into an ANN index with the original text stored alongside. This runs once, and again whenever documents change.
  2. Query path (amber): you embed the question with the same model. The index returns the top-k chunks by cosine similarity. The prompt becomes the question plus those passages.
  3. Grounded answer: the model writes the answer from the passages. Grounding means every claim traces to a retrieved passage. A citation names the source chunk so a human can verify it.

Worked trace (illustrative). A support corpus: 2,000 documents become 24,000 chunks at 400 tokens each with 15 percent overlap. Embedding is one-time, minutes on a GPU.

  1. A user asks "how do SSO users reset passwords".
  2. The query embeds in about 5 ms.
  3. ANN search over 24,000 vectors returns the top 5 in about 20 ms.
  4. The prompt is the question plus 5 passages, roughly 2,000 tokens.
  5. The model answers: "Use the SSO portal link on page 3 of the admin guide," with a citation.
  6. Total added latency over a bare model call: tens of milliseconds plus the longer prompt.

The naive baseline. This exact pipeline, with fixed-size chunks, one embedding model, plain ANN, and no reranker, is the naive baseline. Every advanced RAG technique is a fix to a measured failure of this baseline. Do not add stages until evals show the baseline failing. Each stage adds latency, cost, and new failure modes.

Key takeaways

  • RAG is two paths: index once offline, retrieve and generate per question online.
  • Grounding ties every claim to a passage. Citations make it checkable by a human.
  • Start from the naive baseline. Add stages only where evals show a gap.

Design prompt

  1. "Walk me through both paths of RAG for a 2,000-document support corpus. Where does the latency go?"
  2. "What is the naive baseline, and why do you insist on starting there instead of building the full pipeline first?"

Next: Chapter 5 asks where the naive baseline breaks in production, and names the four classic failures.

Chapter 5

Where naive RAG breaks

The felt problem. The naive baseline works on demos and breaks in production. It breaks in the same four ways, everywhere. Learn the four. Every advanced technique in Path B is one of their fixes.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Missed retrieval: the right page exists but ranks 47th. The answer was in the corpus and the system still failed. Fixes: hybrid search, better chunking, a reranker.
  2. Ignored context: the retriever found the right page. The model answered from memory anyway, contradicting the passage. Faithfulness is the property that the answer stays true to the retrieved passages. Fixes: faithfulness evals, citation requirements in the prompt.
  3. Split facts: the answer spans a chunk boundary. This is the chunking failure from Chapter 3. No retriever can fix it. Fixes: overlap, semantic chunking, parent-child chunking (retrieve small, show large).
  4. Stale index: someone updated the documents and no one rebuilt the index. The system confidently answers from last quarter's policy. Fix: a re-index pipeline with a freshness SLO.

Two quiet killers. Context stuffing: pasting 50 chunks "to be safe" drowns the signal in noise. It multiplies cost, since every token is priced. Permission leaks: a private chunk retrieved for the wrong user. The retriever must only search what the user may read. Filtering after retrieval is too late. Both return in the reading paths. Evals measure stuffing (Path C). Guardrails stop leaks (Path D).

The rule underneath. Retrieval quality caps answer quality. No prompt trick recovers a fact the retriever never returned. That is why Path C (evals) comes before advanced RAG. You cannot fix what you cannot measure.

Key takeaways

  • Four failures: missed retrieval, ignored context, split facts, stale index. Each has a named fix.
  • Faithfulness means the answer stays true to the passages. Measure it. Do not assume it.
  • Retrieval quality caps answer quality. Evals come before fixes.

Design prompt

  1. "Answer quality is poor. Walk me through the four failure modes in order and say how you would distinguish each."
  2. "A private document appears in another user's answer. Where did the pipeline fail, and what is the correct fix?"

Next: Chapter 6 goes beyond answering questions: agents, for work that needs hands, not just knowledge.

Chapter 6

Agents: when retrieval is not enough

The felt gap and RAG answers questions from documents. Real work means doing things: checking the order status in the database, booking the flight, running the analysis, verifying the result before replying. Retrieval gives the model knowledge. It does not give it hands. An agent is a system that gives a language model hands and the judgment to use them. It plans, calls tools, reads the results, and repeats until the job is done.

Tools, defined and A tool is a function the model may call. It has a name, a description of what it does, and a schema for its inputs (the parameter names, their types, which are required). Function calling is the mechanism. The model outputs a structured call instead of text. Your code runs it. The tool result is pasted back into the conversation.

The model never touches the database directly. It asks through the tool, and your code enforces the rules.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Perceive. Read the goal and the current state.
  2. Reason. Decide the next step.
  3. Act. Call a tool.
  4. Observe. Read the tool result. Repeat.
  5. Stop. Step budget, time budget, or loop detection ends the loop.
e>
How to read this diagram.
  1. Perceive: read the goal and the current state. Reason: decide the next step. Act: call a tool. Observe: read the tool result. Repeat.
  2. ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool calls: thought, action, observation, thought, action. Plan-and-execute plans all steps first, then runs them. It is better for long tasks, worse when the world surprises you.
  3. The loop must stop. Four stop conditions: the answer is ready, a step budget ran out (say 10 iterations), a time budget ran out, or loop detection fired (the same failing tool call twice in a row). Without these, the loop burns money forever.
  4. RAG inside the loop: retrieval becomes one tool among many. The agent can retrieve a policy, then check the database, then run code, then verify its own draft against the retrieved passages.

Planning and memory, briefly. Planning is breaking a goal into steps before acting. Memory is what the agent retains across steps.

The conversation history is short-term memory. Notes the agent writes to a store are long-term memory. Both are deep topics. Path A gives them full chapters.

Where this volume goes from here. Part 1 ends here. You now hold the whole map. Part 2 is the reading map through the RRK books.

Path A deepens agents (RRK chapters 3 and 8): the loop, tools, planning patterns, memory layers, multi-agent topologies. Path B deepens RAG (RRK chapters 9, 10, 11): the type ladder, chunking, hybrid search, reranking. A note on order: Part 1 taught RAG before agents because retrieval is the simpler idea. The paths start with agents because agentic RAG assumes the loop. Read the paths in A to F order.

Key takeaways

  • An agent is a language model in a loop with tools. Perceive, reason, act, observe, repeat, with stop conditions.
  • Tools are functions with schemas. Function calling lets the model invoke them without touching systems directly.
  • RAG answers questions. Agents do work. Retrieval becomes one tool inside the loop.

Next: Part 2, the reading paths. Path A deepens the agent loop first, because every other path is one of its components.

Design prompt

  1. "What is an agent, and how is it different from RAG and from a chatbot? When would you NOT use one?"
  2. "Your agent calls the same failing tool repeatedly. Which stop condition fires, and what do you change so it does not happen again?"
Hands-on

Path A: Agents (RRK chapters 3 and 8)

Why the paths start here and Part 1 built the whole map. The paths deepen it. Agents come first because every other path is a component of the agent. RAG is its senses. Evals are its exams. Guardrails are its seatbelts.

Reading order. Read Chapter 3 (Agentic Design Basics, from zero) first, then Chapter 8 (Agents, deeply). Chapter 6 built the loop from zero on this page. RRK ch 3 deepens it.

Master: the perceive-reason-act loop and the three stop conditions (step budget, time budget, loop detection). Tool-calling mechanics. ReAct vs plan-and-execute. The four memory layers. Multi-agent topologies. Context hygiene for the lead agent.

Skim: the ADK mapping section. Learn that every framework renames the same ideas. Do not memorize Google's current product names.

Bridge notes: what the spine adds

Cost per loop iteration (Volume 8) and RRK teaches the loop. Volume 8 prices it. Every iteration is a full forward pass over the entire history, so history growth is cost growth. Latency per loop (Volume 8, Chapter 6). RRK's "6 steps at 2 seconds is a 12-second feature" is a TTFT/TPOT budgeting exercise. Measure it, do not guess it.

KV cache growth (Volume 4, Volume 8 Chapter 3): the history lives in the KV cache. A 10-step agent with 2k tokens of history per step holds far more KV memory than a single chat turn. Long-horizon agents are where paged memory management earns its keep. Planning depth (Volume 7): bounding planning depth is the same instinct as KL constraints in RL. Keep the policy near what you can verify.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Four cards. Each maps one agent-loop cost to a spine volume. Per-iteration cost (Volume 8). TTFT/TPOT latency budgeting (Volume 8, Ch 6). KV cache growth (Volumes 4 and 8). Planning depth as KL-style constraint (Volume 7).
  2. Cost card: every iteration is a full forward pass over the entire history, so history growth is cost growth. Long histories are not free context.
  3. KV card: a 10-step agent with 2k tokens of history per step holds far more KV memory than a single chat turn. This is where paged memory earns its keep.
  4. Teaching point: RRK teaches the loop. The spine prices it. Measure latency, do not guess it. Bound planning depth like you bound a policy.

Worked example: price one agent task (illustrative prices)

An 8-step support agent averages 1,500 tokens of history per step. That is 12,000 tokens total. At an illustrative $3 per million tokens: 12,000 / 1,000,000 x $3 = $0.036 per task. At one million tasks a day that is $36,000 a day. Now apply the spine. Continuous batching (Volume 8, Chapter 2) raises the tokens/s per GPU.

Int4 weights (Volume 8, Chapter 5) halve the memory cost. A draft model (Volume 8, Chapter 6) cuts decode passes. The agent chapter tells you what the loop costs. The serving chapters tell you how to move the cost.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. The circular loop: perceive, reason, act, observe, repeat. The same loop RRK Chapter 3 teaches.
  2. 2. A coin stack sits on each step. Every iteration is a full model call over the full history, so each lap costs tokens times price.
  3. 3. The formula at the bottom: cost per task = steps x tokens per step x price per token.
  4. 4. Teaching point: agent economics are multiplicative. Cutting steps (better planning bounds) and cutting price per token (Volume 8 techniques) multiply together.
Loop
What it is: The perceive-reason-act cycle from RRK Chapter 3. What breaks if it fails: An unbounded loop is an unbounded bill. The three stop conditions are cost controls.
Coin stacks
What it is: Per-iteration model-call cost. What breaks if it fails: Forgetting that history growth raises every later step's cost.
Formula
What it is: The unit economics of one agent task. What breaks if it fails: Optimizing tokens while ignoring steps, or vice versa.

Common misunderstanding.

"More steps make a smarter agent." Error compounds per step. A 95%-reliable step repeated 20 times succeeds about 36% of the time (0.95^20). Depth must be earned with verification at each step (Volume 7's verifier instinct, RRK's stop conditions). Reviewers test this with "your agent runs 50 steps, how do you bound it". The strong answer names step budgets, time budgets, loop detection, and per-step verification. Then it prices the whole thing with the formula above.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Start at Thought. The model looks at what it knows and decides the next move.
  2. The Action is a tool call: search, run code, or hit an API.
  3. The Observation pastes the tool result back into context.
  4. Loop back to Thought. Stop only when the task is done. The three stop conditions are a step budget, a time budget, and loop detection.
How to read this diagram.
  1. The user asks a question. The model answers with a tool_call: structured JSON, not prose.
  2. Your code executes the call: an HTTP request, a database query, a shell command.
  3. The tool result is pasted back into the model's context as an Observation.
  4. The model writes the final answer grounded in the tool output. It never touches the outside world directly.
How to read this diagram.
  1. Left: fixed scaffolding. A prompt chain runs A, then B, then C, every time.
  2. Middle: the model picks. A router chooses the branch. A tool loop chooses which tool and in what order.
  3. Right: the agent plans, acts, and replans on its own.
  4. Rule of thumb from Anthropic: use the simplest pattern that solves the job. More autonomy means more capability and more failure modes.

Design prompt

  1. "What is an agent, and how is it different from a chatbot or a workflow engine? When would you NOT use one?" (G1)
  2. "Your agent is stuck calling the same failing tool over and over. How do you stop that?" (G2)
  3. "One agent or many? How do you split work across sub-agents without drowning the lead agent in context?" (G7, G9)
  4. "When do you use ReAct, reflection, or hierarchical delegation? How do you bound planning depth?" (G8)
  5. "What belongs in short-term memory, long-term memory, or an external system of record?" (G12)
  6. "Price this agent: 10 steps, 2k tokens per step, at $3 per million tokens. Now cut the cost 3x without hurting quality." (Spine bridge: batching, quantization, fewer steps.)

Key line.

"I use an agent only where the number or order of steps cannot be known up front. Every iteration is a full forward pass over the full history. So I bound the loop with step, time, and loop-detection budgets. I verify each step. I price the task as steps times tokens times the per-token price, which I move with batching and quantization."

Key takeaways

  • Read RRK ch 3 then ch 8. Master the loop, stop conditions, tools, planning patterns, memory layers. Skim ADK product names.
  • Bridge: Volume 8 prices each iteration. Volume 4/8 explain why history growth is memory growth.
  • Cost per task = steps x tokens x price. Error compounds per step, so depth must be earned with verification.

Next: Path B, RAG: the retrieval half of the agent's senses, and the four ways naive RAG breaks.

Hands-on

Path B: RAG (RRK chapters 9, 10, 11)

Why this next. Agents need knowledge. RAG is how they get it. Path A built the loop. This path builds the retrieval half of the agent's senses.

Reading order. Read Chapter 9 (RAG types) first, then 10 (chunking), then 11 (embeddings, vector search, reranking). Chapters 2-5 built RAG from zero on this page. RRK ch 9-11 deep en it and master: The naive baseline and what each advanced stage fixes and the modular router idea. Agentic RAG (retrieval as a tool inside the Path A loop). GraphRAG's "retrieve structure, not passages". The chunking trade-offs and the boundary problem. Hybrid dense + BM25 search fused with RRF (reciprocal rank fusion). Reranking as "spend compute where it mat

ters". Skim: the Vertex AI Search / Document AI specifics. Learn what the managed service does, not its console clicks.

Bridge notes: what the spine adds

ANN quantization (Volume 8, Chapter 5). RRK Chapter 11 teaches ScaNN: trees plus quantization that respects the dot product. That is the quantization survey applied to vectors: smaller numbers, cheaper search, same trade-offs. Rerank cost (Volume 8, Chapters 2-3) and A cross-encoder reranker scores each candidate with a full forward pass. Reranking 50 candidates is 50 forward passes. Budget it like a batch and watch the KV math.

Chunking and tokens (Volume 4). You measure chunks in tokens. The embedding model's context limit is a hard wall. Chunking decisions are tokenization decisions. Lost in the middle: stuffing more retrieved passages into the prompt hits the attention dilution the spine built from scratch. Retrieval precision beats context stuffing.

Worked example: a retrieval latency budget (illustrative)

Query embedding 5 ms. ANN search over 10M vectors 20 ms. Fetch 50 candidates 5 ms. Cross-encoder rerank 50 x 6 ms = 300 ms. Prompt build + TTFT 400 ms. Total about 730 ms.

The reranker is 40% of it. The spine instinct: cut rerank candidates to 20 (120 ms) or distill a cheaper reranker. Do not "optimize" the 20 ms ANN search first. Measure the budget the way Volume 8, Chapter 7 demands: fixed queries, p50/p99, not vibes.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Top: the diamond is the query router. It classifies the incoming query.
  2. 2. Four arrows branch to four strategies: naive (simple lookup), advanced (rewrite plus rerank), agentic (the Path A loop calling retrieval as a tool), graph (traverse entity relations).
  3. 3. Teaching point: the router exists because queries differ. A factoid needs naive RAG. A multi-hop question needs agentic or graph retrieval. One pipeline for all queries is the beginner design.
Router
What it is: Per-query strategy selection from RRK Chapter 9. What breaks if it fails: A router with no eval behind it routes by superstition. The eval path (Path C) calibrates it.
Agentic branch
What it is: Retrieval driven by the agent loop from Path A. What breaks if it fails: Every retrieval step multiplies the cost equation from Path A.
Graph branch
What it is: Retrieve structure (entities, relations), not just passages. What breaks if it fails: It needs a knowledge graph built and maintained: the most powerful and most expensive branch.

Common misunderstanding.

"Better embeddings fix bad retrieval." No. Retrieval can only find what chunking preserved. If the answer was split across a chunk boundary or buried in a 2000-token chunk, no embedding model recovers it. RRK Chapter 10's line is "chunking decides everything downstream" and the concise version is S37 (RAG accuracy dropped: diagnose it). The strong answer walks the pipeline in order: chunking, then embeddings, then index, then rerank, then prompt. It measures at each stage, because the failure is usually upstream of where it surfaces.

Design prompt

  1. "Explain RAG, then design production-grade RAG. Answer quality is poor: how do you diagnose it end to end?" (S9, S37)
  2. "RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompting vs deterministic workflow: how do you choose?" (D9)
  3. "Enterprise RAG on 10M documents with sub-2s latency. Walk me through the latency budget." (S36, S13)
  4. "When does GraphRAG beat naive RAG, and what does it cost you?"
  5. "Your reranker is 40% of latency. Give me three ways to cut it and what each sacrifices." (Spine bridge.)
  6. "Design sentence-level citations so the system can reliably say I do not know." (G17)

Key line.

"I start from the naive baseline and add stages only where evals show a gap. Chunking first, because retrieval cannot recover what chunking destroyed. Hybrid search with RRF for recall. A reranker where the latency budget allows, since reranking dominates the budget. A router or agentic retrieval only for query classes that need it, because each adds multiplicative cost."

How to read this diagram.
  1. Index path (offline): source docs are cut into chunks. Each chunk is embedded. The vectors go into an ANN index such as HNSW or IVF.
  2. Query path (online): the user query is embedded. The index returns the top-k passages by vector similarity.
  3. The prompt becomes the question plus the retrieved passages. The LLM writes a grounded answer, ideally with citations.
  4. Failure mode to memorize: retrieval quality caps answer quality. Bad retrieval in, bad answer out.
How to read this diagram.
  1. Fixed-size, no overlap: simple, but it cuts mid-sentence. Ideas that span a boundary are lost.
  2. Fixed-size, with overlap: overlap heals boundary cuts at roughly twice the chunks and index size.
  3. Semantic: cut at sentence or paragraph boundaries. Meaning stays intact, but chunk sizes are uneven and you need a splitter.

Key takeaways

  • Read RRK ch 9, then 10, then 11. Master the type ladder, chunking trade-offs, hybrid search, reranking.
  • Bridge: ScaNN quantization is Volume 8's quantization survey applied to vectors. Rerank cost is a batching problem. Chunks are tokenization decisions.
  • Diagnose RAG failures upstream-first: chunking, embeddings, index, rerank, prompt.

Next: Path C, evals: retrieval and agents both need grading, and eval is how you stop guessing.

Hands-on

Path C: Evals (RRK chapter 12)

Why this next. You can build agents and RAG. Now you must grade them. Chapter 12 is the best chapter in the book for study ROI.

Reading order and Read Chapter 12 straight through. It is the best chapter in the book for study ROI. Master: The one idea (eval is how you stop guessing). RAG metrics. Trajectory eval for agents. Golden-set construction.

llm-as-judge rubrics and their pitfalls. Regression dashboards. Ci gates. And the eval-driven iteration loop.. The commented eval harness is worth typing out by hand.

Bridge notes: what the spine adds

Eval methodology (Volume 2). Leakage, metric selection, and statistical hygiene are spine foundations. RRK's golden sets inherit all of it. Judges and verifiers (Volume 7). RLHF's reward models and RLVR's verifiers are the same idea as LLM-as-judge, with the same failure modes (reward hacking is judge gaming).

Benchmark rigor (Volume 8, Chapter 7). Fix the sampler and seed, report p50/p99, warm up. Every rule applies to eval harnesses too. An eval that changes the sampler between runs measures the sampler, not the system.

Worked example: size the golden set honestly (illustrative)

You want to detect a 5-point accuracy regression. With n = 100 golden tasks, the standard error of a 70% pass rate is about 4.6 points. A 5-point drop is barely distinguishable from noise. With n = 400, the standard error halves to about 2.3 points. The regression becomes detectable. The lesson: small golden sets cannot see small regressions.

Report the set size next to every eval number. Grow the set where the decisions are close.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Clockwise from the top: the golden set (fixed tasks with known-good answers), the run (the system under test), the judge (LLM or rubric scoring), the dashboard (trends and regressions), and iterate (the fix that starts the next lap).
  2. 2. The loop is closed. Every change re-runs the same golden set, so improvements are measured, not felt.
  3. 3. Teaching point: the loop is the product. Teams without it argue about quality. Teams with it read the dashboard. The CI gate is this loop running automatically on every change.
Golden set
What it is: Fixed, versioned tasks with trusted answers. What breaks if it fails: A golden set that never grows goes stale. A golden set with leakage measures memorization.
Judge
What it is: LLM-as-judge with rubrics. What breaks if it fails: Verbose, confident, wrong answers fool lazy judges. Calibrate against human labels.
Dashboard + CI gate
What it is: Trend tracking and automatic blocking of regressions. What breaks if it fails: A dashboard nobody reads is decoration. The gate is what makes it a contract.

Common misunderstanding.

"The LLM judge is ground truth." Judges have systematic biases. They prefer verbose answers. They prefer the first of two options (position bias). They grade their own model family generously. The RRK chapter names the pitfalls. The spine adds the fix: calibrate the judge against human labels, measure agreement, and use verifiers (Volume 7's RLVR instinct) wherever the answer is checkable.

The classic trap is G15: pass@k vs pass^k, trajectory vs final answer. The strong answer: score the trajectory, not just the destination, because agents fail in the middle.

Design prompt

  1. "Pass@k vs pass^k: what does each measure, and which do you report for an agent?" (G15)
  2. "Design the eval harness for an agent product: dimensions, eval set construction, CI gates." (G33, S8)
  3. "Your LLM judge disagrees with humans 30% of the time. What do you do?" (Calibrate, rubric, verifier.)
  4. "When is synthetic eval data appropriate, and how do you know it has not made your benchmark unrealistic?" (G39)
  5. "How do you measure continuous improvement without reinforcing bad behavior?" (G34)

Key line.

"Eval is how I stop guessing. A versioned golden set. Trajectory scoring for agents because they fail in the middle. An LLM judge calibrated against human labels, since judges have position and verbosity biases. The whole loop behind a CI gate, so regressions block the deploy instead of becoming incidents."

Key takeaways

  • Read RRK ch 12 fully and type out the eval harness. Master golden sets, judge pitfalls, trajectory eval, CI gates.
  • Bridge: Volume 2 gives the methodology. Volume 7 gives judges/verifiers. Volume 8 gives measurement rigor.
  • Size the golden set to the decision. n=100 cannot see a 5-point regression. Report n next to every number.

Next: Path D, guardrails: graded systems still face adversaries.

Hands-on

Path D: Guardrails, security, tenancy (RRK chapter 13)

Why this next. A system that works is not a system that is safe. Chapter 13 layers defenses, because every single layer fails.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Input screening. First filter on the prompt.
  2. Injection detection. Catch prompt-injection and jailbreaks.
  3. PII redaction. Remove personal data before it spreads.
  4. Permission filter. Pre-retrieval: never let forbidden content enter context.
  5. Human approval. Gates before any irreversible action.
  6. Audit trail. Tamper-evident log of what happened.
How to read this diagram.
  1. Green card: the safe order. The permission filter runs before retrieval, so the retriever only sees documents the user may see. Nothing leaks downstream.
  2. Red card: the leaky order. Post-retrieval filtering leaks through timing differences, through citations, and through I-can't-show-you-that confirmations.
  3. Amber panel: agents raise the stakes. A chatbot's worst case is a bad answer. An agent's worst case is a wrong tool call. Write actions sit behind human approval gates. Reliability contracts give each guardrail an SLO, a test, and a trace.

Reading order. Read Chapter 13 straight through and master: The one idea (layers, because every single layer fails) and prompt-injection and jailbreak attack classes. PII detection and redaction. Pre-retrieval vs post-retrieval permission filtering and the leak. Multi-tenant isolation. Audit logging. Human approval gates for write actions.

Bridge notes: what the spine adds

Reliability contracts (Volume 10, Chapter 9) and RRK's layers become Volume 10's verifiable contracts. Each guardrail gets an SLO, a test, and a trace. Permission filtering and the leak: filter before retrieval (never retrieve what the user may not see). Post-retrieval filtering leaks through timing, citations, and "I can't show you that" confirmations. This is the single most-tested guardrail idea in enterprise design reviews. Agents raise the stakes (Path A): a chatbot's worst case is a bad answer.

An agent's worst case is a wrong tool call. That is why write actions sit behind human approval gates.

Worked example: the permission leak, concretely

A support agent retrieves from a shared drive. Pre-retrieval filtering: the retriever only searches documents the user is allowed to read, so forbidden content never enters the context. Post-retrieval filtering: the retriever searches everything, then a filter strips forbidden chunks before generation. The leak: the model says "I found 3 relevant documents but can only show you 2," confirming the forbidden document exists. Or latency differs measurably. The fix is architectural (filter at retrieval), not a better prompt.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Top to bottom: input filter, injection screen, PII redaction, permission check, audit log. The request arrow passes through every layer.
  2. 2. Each layer is a different color because each is a different mechanism. No single technology covers all five.
  3. 3. Teaching point: layers exist because every layer fails. The key sentence is the chapter's one idea. You do not pick the best layer. You stack them and monitor each one's catch rate.
Injection screen
What it is: Prompt-injection and jailbreak detection. What breaks if it fails: Attackers evolve past static patterns. The screen needs its own eval loop (Path C).
Permission check
What it is: Pre-retrieval access filtering. What breaks if it fails: Placed after retrieval it leaks existence. Placement is the design decision.
Audit log
What it is: Tamper-evident record of what the system did. What breaks if it fails: The layer that saves you in the incident review (Volume 10, Chapter 7).

Common misunderstanding.

"Our prompt says not to reveal secrets, so we are safe." A prompt instruction is not a security boundary. It is a suggestion the model weighs against the attacker's instructions. Real boundaries are architectural: permission filtering at retrieval, approval gates before writes, PII redaction before logging. Reviewers test this with "the model was told not to, but it did". The strong answer never trusts the model to enforce policy against an adversary.

Design prompt

  1. "Design secure agent tool-calling: auth, least privilege, consent, token handling." (G27)
  2. "A customer agent calls internal APIs under the user\u2019s permissions. Where do you enforce them and why?" (S26)
  3. "Pre-retrieval vs post-retrieval permission filtering: which leaks, and how?"
  4. "When does a write action need a human approval gate, and what belongs in the audit log?" (G4)

Key line.

"I stack guardrails in layers because every single layer fails. Input screening. Injection detection. PII redaction. Pre-retrieval permission filtering, so forbidden content never enters context. Human approval gates before any write action.

A tamper-evident audit log. Policy is enforced by architecture, never by asking the model nicely."

Key takeaways

  • Read RRK ch 13 fully. Master layered defense, injection classes, the permission-filtering leak, approval gates, audit logging.
  • Bridge: Volume 10 turns layers into verifiable reliability contracts. Path A explains why agents need stronger gates than chatbots.
  • Enforce policy with architecture (retrieval filtering, approval gates), not with prompts.

Next: Path E, the FDE playbook: the chapter that teaches you to think like an L6.

Hands-on

Path E: The FDE playbook (RRK chapter 4)

Why this next. You know the components. Now learn the job. Chapter 4 is the "think like an L6" chapter: discovery, SLOs, evals, unit economics, build vs buy.

Reading order. Read Chapter 4 straight through. It is the "think like an L6" chapter and master: Discovery questioning. Reliability as SLOs and error budgets. Evaluation with golden sets and LLM-as-judge. The productionizing gap (demo to prod). The worked unit-economics example of the support agent. The build-vs-buy decisi

on framework. Skim: the GCP product-name specifics inside "cloud tooling fluency". Learn the workshop categories: compute, messaging, storage, eval, deploy.

Bridge notes: what the spine adds

Unit economics (Volume 8 + Volume 10, Chapter 8) and RRK works the support-agent cost end to end and the spine gives you the levers that move it. Batching and quantization set the per-token price (Volume 8). Volume 10 prices the whole system including people and incidents. Error budgets (Volume 10, Chapter 9). RRK introduces SLOs. Volume 10 makes them contracts with verification and replay.

Evaluation (Paths A-C): the playbook's "evaluate" step is Paths B and C applied. Golden sets for the RAG parts, trajectory eval for the agent parts.

Worked example: extend RRK's unit economics with spine levers (illustrative)

RRK's support agent costs $0.036 per task at $3 per million tokens (Path A math). Apply three spine levers. Continuous batching doubles tokens/s per GPU (halves compute cost per token). Int4 weights halve memory (fewer GPUs per replica). A draft model cuts decode passes ~2x (Volume 8, Chapter 6). Combined, the per-token price falls toward $1 per million: $0.012 per task.

The lesson reviewers want: cost is a design output, not a bill you read later. You change the architecture, then re-read the unit economics.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Left column: the RRK concepts (agents, RAG, evals, cost). Right column: the spine volumes (KV cache, ANN search, judge evals, unit economics).
  2. 2. Curved orange arrows pair them. Agents pair with KV cache cost. RAG pairs with ANN search quantization. Evals pair with judge methodology. Cost pairs with unit economics.
  3. 3. Teaching point: the pairing is the study strategy. When RRK says a thing costs or scales, the arrow tells you which spine volume proves it. Read them as one system, not two books.
Left column
What it is: RRK v2 concepts from Paths A through E. What breaks if it fails: Reading them without the spine leaves the numbers unpriced and the mechanisms unproven.
Right column
What it is: Spine volumes 2, 4, 7, 8, 10. What breaks if it fails: Reading them without RRK leaves first principles with no production shape.
Arrows
What it is: The bridge notes in each path. What breaks if it fails: The arrows are the highest-ROI lines in this volume. They turn two books into one mental model.

Common misunderstanding.

"The demo is the product." The playbook's productionizing section exists because demos hide everything expensive: no evals, no guardrails, no cost math, no on-call. The concise version is D16 ("define POC success so the demo is not impressive but unusable") and H2 (a launch that went badly). The strong answer names the productionizing checklist before being asked: evals, guardrails, cost, monitoring, rollback, and an owner.

Design prompt

  1. "RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompting vs workflow vs no LLM: how do you choose?" (D9)
  2. "Explain to a CFO why the model gives different results each run, and why that is not a bug." (D20)
  3. "Five levers to cut LLM cost 10x without destroying quality." (G35)
  4. "What is cost per completed task, not just cost per token? How would you impose budgets?" (G36)
  5. "Build vs buy: hosted APIs vs self-hosted open weights for an enterprise customer." (S39)
  6. "The customer insists on GenAI for what is really a rules problem. What do you do?" (D10)

Key line.

"I estimate before I build. Discovery first, then the unit economics per completed task, then evals as the contract, then the build. Cost is a design output, so I move it with batching, quantization, and speculation, and I re-price after every architectural change. And I never let a demo set expectations a production system has to keep."

Key takeaways

  • Read RRK ch 4 fully. Master discovery, SLOs/error budgets, unit economics, build vs buy.
  • Bridge: Volume 8 gives the cost levers. Volume 10 turns SLOs into contracts.
  • Cost per completed task is the metric. Re-price after every architectural change.

Next: Path F, GPUs, serving, and the GCP stack: the infrastructure everything above runs on.

Hands-on

Path F: GPUs, serving, and the GCP stack (RRK chapters 14 and 5)

Why this next. Every loop iteration costs tokens, memory, and milliseconds. Chapter 14 prices them. Chapter 5 puts the whole stack on GCP.

Reading order. Read Chapter 14 (GPUs, serving, cost math) first, then Chapter 5 (GCP for agentic AI, end to end).

Master in ch 14: the one idea (cost is a design constraint), the quantization and batching summaries (now with Volume 8's math behind them), the throughput-vs-latency knee, and the cost-math worked examples.

Master in ch 5: the portable architecture and where compute runs. How messaging and orchestration connect it. Where data lands. Where the agent stack lives. The two reference architectures (production RAG agent; multi-agent system). Skim: individual GCP product names and console flows.

Bridge notes: what the spine adds

Volume 8 deepens all of Chapter 14. RRK's quantization section becomes Volume 8, Chapter 5 (GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF/QAT with what-breaks-where). The batching knee becomes Volume 8, Chapter 2 with worked math. The cost examples become Volume 10, Chapter 8's unit economics. Read RRK 14 as the FDE-flavored summary, then prove each claim in the spine.

Chapter 5 maps to Volume 10. RRK's observability section (metrics, logs, traces for agents) is Volume 10, Chapter 3's monitoring. The delivery section (shipping safely) is Volume 10, Chapter 6's shadow/canary rollout. The reference architectures are the worked examples Volume 13 (system design) will ask you to draw on a whiteboard.

The portable reference architecture (reconstructed from RRK ch 5)

USER REQUEST
    |
[API GATEWAY] -- auth, rate limits, tenant routing
    |
[ORCHESTRATOR] -- the agent loop (Path A): plans, calls tools
    |     |
    |   [TOOL BUS] -- search, SQL, internal APIs (each with timeouts)
    |
[RETRIEVAL] -- embed -> vector search -> rerank (Path B)
    |
[GUARDRAILS] -- input screen, PII redact, permission filter (Path D)
    |
[MODEL SERVING] -- batched, quantized, spec-decoded (Volume 8)
    |
[OBSERVABILITY] -- traces, token/cost meters, eval scores (Path C)
    |
[DATA PLANE] -- sessions, memory, audit log, golden sets

Read it top to bottom as the request's journey, then bottom to top as the dependencies. The data plane (sessions, audit log) must exist before the orchestrator is trustworthy. Every box is one path from this guide. That is the point. In the review you draw these boxes with opinions: which box you would build first, which you would buy, and where the eval gate sits.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Top to bottom: the request's journey: API gateway (auth, rate limits, tenant routing), orchestrator (the agent loop), tool bus, retrieval, guardrails, model serving, observability, data plane.
  2. Bottom to top: the dependencies. The data plane (sessions, audit log, golden sets) must exist before the orchestrator is trustworthy.
  3. Teaching point: every box is one path from this guide. Product names churn; the boxes do not. In the review you draw these boxes with opinions: which to build first, which to buy, and where the eval gate sits.

Common misunderstanding.

"Learning the cloud console is learning the architecture." Product names churn; the boxes do not. Reviewers test the portable pattern: "walk me through building this on any cloud" (the RRK G-bank style, e.g. S22). The strong answer draws the gateway, orchestrator, retrieval, guardrails, serving, observability, and data plane. Then it maps each to whatever the shop uses. Memorize the boxes and their contracts.

Look up the SKUs when hired.

Design prompt

  1. "Walk me through building an enterprise agent on the cloud: where do sessions, the runner, and memory live?" (S22 style)
  2. "Cloud Run vs GKE vs VMs for serving: how do you choose?" (S20)
  3. "Design an end-to-end ML pipeline: training, serving, monitoring, drift." (S14)
  4. "Multi-tenant chatbot platform: ingestion, RAG, rerank, tenant isolation, eval pipeline." (S16)
  5. "Your GPU bill tripled. Walk me through the diagnosis using the cost-math framework." (S42 style)

Key line.

"I draw the system as portable boxes: gateway, orchestrator, tool bus, retrieval, guardrails, model serving, observability, data plane. Each box has a contract and an eval gate. I can map the boxes to any cloud's products. I price the serving box with batching, quantization, and the latency-throughput knee. I do this before I pick hardware."

Key takeaways

  • Read RRK ch 14 then ch 5. Master the cost-math framework and the portable architecture. Skim product names.
  • Bridge: Volume 8 proves ch 14's claims. Volume 10 implements ch 5's observability and delivery sections.
  • Draw boxes with opinions in design reviews: build vs buy per box, eval gate placement, cost per box.

Interview sentence bank (say these out loud)

  • "I use an agent only where the number or order of steps cannot be known up front."
  • "Every loop iteration is a full forward pass over the full history, so I budget steps, time, and loop detection."
  • "Chunking decides everything downstream: retrieval cannot recover what chunking destroyed."
  • "Eval is how I stop guessing: golden sets, trajectory scoring, a calibrated judge, and a CI gate."
  • "Layers, because every single layer fails: policy is enforced by architecture, not by prompts."
  • "Cost is a design output: I move it with batching, quantization, and speculation, then re-price."
  • "I operate left of the latency-throughput knee and scale out for throughput."

Key takeaways

  • Two weeks, two hours a day, paths A through F in order, then gaps and question drills.
  • The QA Bank codes in each path's Design prompt set are your drill list.
  • Say the sentence bank out loud until it sounds like you, not like a book.

Next: Appendix 9A, agent evals: the hands-on machinery behind Path C, harnesses, graders, and calibration.

Appendix 9A: Agent Evals

Why this appendix. Path C taught the one idea (eval is how you stop guessing) and the metrics. This appendix builds the machinery and the harness that runs agents. The graders that score them. The calibration that keeps judges honest. The patches production demands.

Chapter 1: Task harnesses

Why this next. Path C said eval is how you stop guessing. The harness is where that starts. It is the examiner, the route, and the notebook, built before any grader scores anything.

Step 1: the idea in one picture

Picture a driving test. The examiner picks the route, sits in the car, watches every turn, and writes down what happened. The examiner is not the student. The route is the same for every student.

A task harness is the examiner, the route, and the dashcam in one program. It runs your agent against a task and records everything. The task definition says what "done" means. The environment holds the files, tools, and fake services. The recorder captures every model call, tool call, and timestamp. The agent plugs in.

The harness runs it the same way every time.

The harness and the agent are separate programs. That separation is the whole point. You can swap in a new model, a new prompt, or a new tool set and compare fairly.

Step 2: why you need one

Agents are noisy. Run the same agent on the same task five times. You may get three passes and two fails. Without a harness you cannot tell whether a change helped or you just got lucky. With one, every experiment is reproducible: same task, same tools, same seed, same timeout. "Did the new prompt help" gets a number instead of a feeling.

A harness also blocks the three classic eval lies. The leaked task: the agent saw the answer in training or in a previous run. The harness resets state so every attempt starts clean. The helpful environment: a tool accidentally returns exactly what the agent needs. The harness uses fixed fixtures and mocked services with documented behavior. The silent mutation: run 3 changes a file that run 4 depends on.

The harness isolates side effects with a fresh sandbox per attempt.

One reporting rule to memorize: every eval number you publish names the harness version and the seed. Two teams running the same agent get different numbers when their harnesses define different realities.

Step 3: the five parts

A minimal harness has five parts. Each one enforces one isolation.

  1. Task spec. A small data structure: an id, the agent's prompt, the starting state (files, database rows, mock responses), and a pointer to the grader. The grader is the program that scores the attempt (Chapter 2 covers it). The agent never sees the grader.
  2. Environment fixture. Before each attempt, a fresh world: fixture files copied to a temp directory, a seeded random number generator, mock services started, the clock set. Torn down afterward. Fixtures live in version control like code, so the world is reviewable.
  3. Tool sandbox. The agent's tools run inside the harness, never against your real systems. A "send email" tool writes to a log instead of sending mail. A "database query" tool hits a throwaway database. Every call is logged with its arguments and result. One attempt's side effects can never leak into the next.
  4. Execution loop with limits. A step budget (say 25 tool calls) and a wall-clock timeout. An agent that loops forever gets a timeout verdict, not an infinite bill.
  5. Trajectory recorder. Every step is recorded: model input, model output, tool called, tool result, time. This record is the trajectory. Graders read it. You replay it when debugging.

Worked example: a harness for a file-organizer agent

The task: an agent receives a messy directory with 40 files and must sort them into folders by type (images, documents, code). The grader checks the final directory tree. Here is a complete minimal harness in Python.

import json
import os
import random
import shutil
import tempfile
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

# A Task bundles everything the agent may see plus a pointer to the grader.
# The agent never sees the grader or the expected answer. That separation
# is what makes the measurement honest. If the agent could read the grader,
# it could game it instead of solving the task.
@dataclass
class Task:
    task_id: str          # stable id, used in reports and regression tracking
    prompt: str           # the exact instruction the agent receives
    fixture_files: dict   # filename -> bytes; the messy starting directory
    grader_name: str      # which grader to run afterward (by name, not code)


# A Step records one action inside an attempt. The full list of steps is the
# trajectory. Trajectories are the raw material for graders, debugging, and
# the trajectory checks in Chapter 4. Complexity: O(1) per recorded step.
@dataclass
class Step:
    kind: str             # "model" | "tool" | "verdict"
    detail: dict          # free-form payload: tool name, args, result, ...
    at: float = field(default_factory=time.time)


class Harness:
    """Runs an agent against tasks with full isolation between attempts.

    The harness owns the sandbox directory, the seeded RNG, the step budget,
    and the clock. The agent only sees `act(prompt, tools)`. This boundary is
    the whole point: nothing about the measurement can leak into the run.
    """

    def __init__(self, seed=0, max_steps=25, timeout_s=120):
        # Fixed seed => the same attempt number always builds the same world.
        # Change the seed and you get a fresh world; keep it and runs repeat.
        self.seed = seed
        self.max_steps = max_steps      # step budget stops infinite loops
        self.timeout_s = timeout_s      # wall-clock cap stops runaway cost
        self.trajectory = []

    def _build_world(self, task, attempt):
        # Fresh temp dir per attempt: attempt N can never see attempt N-1's
        # files. Using tempfile means the OS guarantees a unique path, and
        # cleanup in `finally` below guarantees no leftovers. Break this and
        # you get the "silent mutation" lie from the Why section.
        workdir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix=f"harness_{task.task_id}_")
        for name, data in task.fixture_files.items():
            path = os.path.join(workdir, name)
            os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist_ok=True)
            with open(path, "wb") as f:
                f.write(data)
        # Per-attempt RNG stream: attempt 3 is reproducible on its own.
        rng = random.Random(self.seed + attempt)
        return workdir, rng

    def _sandbox_tools(self, workdir):
        # Tools are plain Python functions closed over the sandbox dir, so the
        # agent physically cannot touch anything outside workdir. This is the
        # "typed allowlisted tools" idea from Supplement B, applied to evals.
        def list_files():
            """List files in the sandbox, relative names only."""
            out = []
            for root, _, files in os.walk(workdir):
                for fn in files:
                    out.append(os.path.relpath(os.path.join(root, fn), workdir))
            return sorted(out)

        def move_file(src, dest):
            """Move one file inside the sandbox. No absolute paths allowed."""
            # Rejecting ".." and absolute paths keeps the agent inside the
            # sandbox even if it tries to escape. Security and eval hygiene
            # are the same mechanism here.
            if os.path.isabs(src) or os.path.isabs(dest) or ".." in src + dest:
                raise ValueError("paths must stay inside the sandbox")
            os.makedirs(os.path.join(workdir, os.path.dirname(dest)), exist_ok=True)
            shutil.move(os.path.join(workdir, src), os.path.join(workdir, dest))
            return f"moved {src} -> {dest}"

        return {"list_files": list_files, "move_file": move_file}

    def run(self, task, agent, attempt=0):
        """Run one attempt. Returns (final_state, trajectory)."""
        workdir, rng = self._build_world(task, attempt)
        tools = self._sandbox_tools(workdir)
        self.trajectory = []
        deadline = time.time() + self.timeout_s
        try:
            # The agent loop: the harness drives, the agent decides.
            # The harness never interprets tool results for the agent; it
            # only records them. Interpretation belongs to the grader.
            for step_i in range(self.max_steps):
                if time.time() > deadline:
                    self.trajectory.append(Step("verdict", {"timeout": True}))
                    break
                # One agent turn: it sees the prompt, the tool list, and the
                # history so far, and returns either a tool call or "done".
                action = agent.act(task.prompt, tools, self.trajectory, rng)
                if action["type"] == "done":
                    break
                # The harness executes the tool, never the agent. This keeps
                # side effects inside the sandbox and inside the log.
                result = tools[action["tool"]](**action["args"])
                self.trajectory.append(Step("tool", {
                    "tool": action["tool"], "args": action["args"],
                    "result": str(result)[:500], "step": step_i,
                }))
            final_state = self._snapshot(workdir)
            return final_state, list(self.trajectory)
        finally:
            # Always clean up, even on timeout or crash. A harness that leaks
            # temp dirs will eventually fill the disk and poison later runs.
            shutil.rmtree(workdir, ignore_errors=True)

    def _snapshot(self, workdir):
        # The grader sees this snapshot, not the live directory. Freezing the
        # final state as data keeps grading deterministic and replayable.
        tree = []
        for root, _, files in os.walk(workdir):
            for fn in sorted(files):
                tree.append(os.path.relpath(os.path.join(root, fn), workdir))
        return {"files": sorted(tree)}


# A stub agent so the harness is runnable end to end. Real agents plug in
# through the same `act` interface: prompt, tools, history, rng in; an
# action dict out. Swapping agents never touches harness code.
class NaiveOrganizer:
    def act(self, prompt, tools, history, rng):
        if not history:
            return {"type": "tool", "tool": "list_files", "args": {}}
        # Toy policy: move every file into a folder named by its extension.
        # A real agent would call the model here; the harness does not care.
        seen = {s.detail["tool"] for s in history if s.kind == "tool"}
        if "list_files" in seen and not any(
                s.detail.get("tool") == "move_file" for s in history):
            files = eval(history[0].detail["result"])
            if files:
                f = files[0]
                ext = os.path.splitext(f)[1].lstrip(".") or "misc"
                return {"type": "tool", "tool": "move_file",
                        "args": {"src": f, "dest": f"{ext}/{os.path.basename(f)}"}}
        return {"type": "done"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Fixture: 4 messy files. In a real suite this would be 40+ files and the
    # fixture would live in version control next to the task spec.
    task = Task(
        task_id="organize-001",
        prompt="Sort every file into a folder named by its extension.",
        fixture_files={"a.png": b"x", "b.png": b"x", "c.py": b"x", "notes.txt": b"x"},
        grader_name="extension_folders",
    )
    h = Harness(seed=7, max_steps=25, timeout_s=30)
    final, traj = h.run(task, NaiveOrganizer(), attempt=0)
    print(json.dumps(final, indent=2))
    print(f"recorded {len(traj)} steps")

How to read this diagram.
  1. Task holds the prompt, fixture files, and grader name. The agent never sees the grader.
  2. Harness.run builds a fresh world per attempt: new temp dir, seeded RNG, sandboxed tools.
  3. The agent loop runs up to max_steps turns or until the timeout. Each tool call is logged as a Step.
  4. Tools are closures over workdir. The agent cannot reach outside the sandbox.
  5. finally wipes the temp dir. No leaks between attempts.
  6. The grader (Chapter 2) receives the frozen final_state snapshot, never the live directory.

The harness, drawn

How to read this diagram.
  1. Start at the task spec on the left. It feeds the harness, never the agent directly.
  2. The harness builds a fresh sandbox: new directory, seeded random numbers.
  3. The agent loop runs inside the sandbox. Every action is recorded.
  4. When the budget or timeout hits, the harness freezes the final state.
  5. The grader reads the trajectory and the snapshot, then emits the verdict.
  6. Notice the one-way arrows. Information flows forward only. The agent never sees the grader.

Common misunderstanding

"The harness is just a test runner." A test runner executes assertions. A harness defines the reality the agent operates in: the tools, the fixtures, the seeds, the timeouts, the isolation. Two teams can run the same agent and get different numbers because their harnesses define different realities. When you read an eval number, ask for the harness version first.

Lab 9A.1: Build a minimal harness
  1. Copy the Harness class above into a new file. Delete NaiveOrganizer.
  2. Write a RandomMover agent. On each turn it picks a random file and a random destination folder using the provided rng. Run 5 attempts with different attempt numbers and the same seed. Confirm the trajectories differ across attempts but each attempt repeats exactly when re-run.
  3. Now break isolation on purpose. Change _build_world to reuse one fixed directory instead of a temp dir. Run the same 5 attempts. Watch attempt 2 see attempt 1's leftovers. This is the silent-mutation lie. Revert the change.
  4. Add a third tool, read_file(name), that returns file bytes. Keep it inside the sandbox the same way.

Next: Chapter 2, graders and rubrics: the harness records what happened; the grader decides whether it was good.

Chapter 2: Graders and rubrics

Why this next. The harness runs the agent and records the trajectory. Someone must decide whether it was good. That someone is the grader. Trajectory plus final state in, score out.

Step 1: the idea in one picture

The harness runs the agent and records what happened. The grader decides whether it was good. A grader is a function. Trajectory plus final state in, score out. Nothing more.

There are two families. An outcome grader looks only at the final state: are the files sorted, is the database row right, did the email contain the facts. A trajectory grader reads the recorded steps: did the agent verify before writing, did it touch anything forbidden.

And there are two builders. Rule-based graders are code with assertions. Model-based graders are LLM judges with rubrics. Most real suites use both. Fast code checks for what is checkable, judges for what is not.

Step 2: why the grader is the eval

A task without a grader is a demo, not an eval. The grader is where your definition of "good" lives. Every definition has sharp edges. A grader that only checks the final answer will pass an agent that got there by luck or by cheating.

Graders also decide what your team optimizes. Agents hill-climb on whatever the grader rewards. Reward short trajectories and you get agents that skip verification. Write the grader first. Then check that the behavior it rewards is the behavior you want.

Step 3: the climb from code to judgment

Build graders in this order, from cheapest to most judgment-heavy. Code first, judges last.

Rung 1: outcome units. Small, independent, checkable units. Each tests one fact and returns pass or fail with a reason. For the file-organizer: every file placed, folders match extensions, no data loss. Independent units give partial credit and precise debugging. "2 of 3 units passed" tells you exactly what broke.

Units must be idempotent: same final state in, same score out, every time. No randomness, no network, no timestamps in the assertions.

Rung 2: trajectory milestones and Scan the recorded steps for required or forbidden events. The agent called read_calendar before book_flight. The agent never called delete_database. Verification happened after the last write, not before. Milestones are cheaper and more stable than full-trajectory judging. You do not need a model to check "was tool X called with argument Y".

Rung 3: rubrics. When a human or an LLM judge grades, they need a rubric: criteria, each with a scale and anchors. An anchor is a concrete example of what each score looks like. Without anchors, two graders reading the same rubric give different scores. A criterion has four parts: the name, what it measures, the scale (say 0 to 2), and one anchor per level. Keep criteria independent. "Correctness" and "completeness" should not both punish the same mistake.

How to read this diagram.
  1. Rung 1: Outcome. Did it work? The final answer or state.
  2. Rung 2: Trajectory. Milestones in the steps. Required or forbidden events.
  3. Rung 3: Rubrics. Graded criteria with written anchors.
  4. Rung 4: LLM Judge. Calibrated against humans. Not ground truth.

Worked example: a grader for a SQL-writing agent

Task: the agent gets a question in English and a database schema, and must return a SQL query. The grader checks the query without trusting the agent's formatting.

import re
import sqlite3

# An outcome grader built from independent checkable units. Each unit is a
# small function returning (passed: bool, reason: str). The grader aggregates.
# Units are idempotent: same database state + same query => same verdict, every
# time. That property is what lets this grader run in CI without flakiness.


def make_test_db():
    # In-memory SQLite: fast, isolated, no server to clean up. Each grading
    # call gets a brand-new database, so one task's rows can never leak into
    # another's. Complexity of setup is O(rows inserted).
    conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    conn.executescript("""
        CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER, customer TEXT, total REAL, status TEXT);
        INSERT INTO orders VALUES
          (1, 'ana', 120.0, 'paid'),
          (2, 'bob',  45.0, 'pending'),
          (3, 'ana',  80.0, 'paid'),
          (4, 'cid', 200.0, 'paid');
    """)
    return conn


def unit_valid_sql(query):
    # Unit 1: does it parse? We ask SQLite to plan the query without running
    # it. EXPLAIN never executes, so a malicious query cannot do damage here.
    # What breaks if changed: skipping this lets syntax errors crash later
    # units with confusing tracebacks instead of a clean "invalid SQL".
    try:
        conn = make_test_db()
        conn.execute("EXPLAIN " + query)
        return True, "parses"
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - any parse failure is a fail
        return False, f"invalid SQL: {e}"


def unit_correct_rows(query, expected_rows):
    # Unit 2: does it return the right rows? We compare sets of tuples, so
    # column order and row order do not matter. Set comparison is O(n) and
    # immune to the agent's formatting choices. What breaks if changed: list
    # comparison would fail correct queries that order rows differently.
    conn = make_test_db()
    try:
        got = set(conn.execute(query).fetchall())
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
        return False, f"execution failed: {e}"
    if got == set(expected_rows):
        return True, f"{len(got)} correct rows"
    return False, f"got {sorted(got)}, expected {sorted(expected_rows)}"


def unit_read_only(query):
    # Unit 3: is it read-only? A SELECT-only agent must never mutate the
    # database. We check the first keyword. This is intentionally strict:
    # WITH ... UPDATE tricks are out of scope for this task's threat model,
    # and the simplicity keeps the unit auditable. See Supplement B Ch 1 for
    # the deeper capability-layer version of this idea.
    first = query.strip().split()[0].upper() if query.strip() else ""
    if first in ("SELECT", "WITH"):
        return True, "read-only"
    return False, f"non-read statement: {first}"


def unit_no_wildcard_dump(query):
    # Unit 4: did it avoid SELECT *? Dumping whole tables is a data-exposure
    # smell. This is a style/correctness hybrid: the task asks for specific
    # columns, so SELECT * is wrong here even when the rows happen to match.
    if re.search(r"select\s+\*", query, re.IGNORECASE):
        return False, "SELECT * dumps whole rows; name the columns"
    return True, "columns named explicitly"


def grade_sql(query, expected_rows):
    # The grader runs units in dependency order: cheap structural checks
    # first, expensive semantic checks later. If the SQL does not parse there
    # is no point running it. Short-circuiting keeps failures fast and the
    # reasons precise. Returns a dict a report can render directly.
    units = [
        ("valid_sql", lambda: unit_valid_sql(query)),
        ("read_only", lambda: unit_read_only(query)),
        ("no_wildcard", lambda: unit_no_wildcard_dump(query)),
        ("correct_rows", lambda: unit_correct_rows(query, expected_rows)),
    ]
    results = {}
    for name, fn in units:
        passed, reason = fn()
        results[name] = {"passed": passed, "reason": reason}
        # Stop after a structural failure: later units would produce noise.
        # This ordering (structure before semantics) is a deliberate design
        # choice. Reversing it gives confusing "wrong rows" reports for
        # queries that never parsed.
        if not passed and name in ("valid_sql",):
            break
    results["score"] = sum(1 for r in results.values()
                           if isinstance(r, dict) and r["passed"]) / len(units)
    return results


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Worked numbers: total paid per customer? Expected: ana 200.0.
    expected = [("ana", 200.0)]
    good = ("SELECT customer, SUM(total) FROM orders "
            "WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY customer HAVING customer='ana'")
    bad = "SELECT * FROM orders"
    print("good query:", grade_sql(good, expected)["score"])  # 1.0
    print("bad query: ", grade_sql(bad, expected)["score"])   # 0.25

How to read this diagram.
  1. make_test_db builds a fresh in-memory database per grading call. No shared state.
  2. Units run in dependency order: parse first, then safety, then semantics. Structural failures short-circuit.
  3. unit_correct_rows compares sets of tuples. Row order and column order do not matter.
  4. unit_read_only is intentionally strict. Auditable beats clever.
  5. The final score is the fraction of units passed, with per-unit reasons for debugging.
  6. The bad query scores 0.25. It parses, but it is not read-only-safe in spirit (SELECT *), and the rows are wrong.

Graders, drawn

How to read this diagram.
  1. The trajectory and final state enter on the left and split three ways.
  2. The outcome grader checks facts about the final state with code.
  3. The trajectory grader checks required and forbidden events in the steps with code.
  4. The LLM judge handles the rest, guided by a rubric with anchors (Chapter 3 calibrates it).
  5. The aggregator combines the three into one verdict with per-unit reasons, never just a number.

A rubric, concretely

For the SQL task, the "query quality" criterion an LLM judge might score.

  • Criterion: Clarity of intent. Does the query express one clear question?
  • Scale: 0 to 2.
  • Anchor for 2: SELECT customer, SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY customer. One question, named columns, filter before grouping.
  • Anchor for 1: Correct result but SELECT * with filtering in Python afterwards. Right answer, wrong division of labor.
